title: Schemas, Connect and change data capture
goal: By the end you can explain how Kafka Connect and Debezium run lesson 1's change data capture for a whole database, why change events need a schema registry and which compatibility mode suits a CDC topic and which an event topic, and publish a database write to Kafka exactly when it commits, with the transactional outbox.

warmup.q: The payment service inserts a payment into PostgreSQL and then calls `producer.send(PaymentAuthorized)`. Which change makes the event reach Kafka if and only if the payment commits?
options: Wrap the insert and the send in a Kafka transaction
Send first, then insert, and retry the send until it succeeds
Insert an outbox row in the same database transaction as the payment, and let Debezium publish it from the WAL
Turn on the idempotent producer
warmup.why: The outbox makes it one write to one database: the payment and its event row commit together or not at all, and Debezium publishes only committed rows, in commit order. A Kafka transaction covers Kafka writes and offsets, never the database (KIP-939's two-phase commit hasn't shipped). Sending first announces payments that may never commit, and retries can't tell which half happened after a crash. The idempotent producer removes duplicates from producer retries; it doesn't tie the send to the database.

sections.h: Kafka Connect runs lesson 1's follower for a whole database
sections.body:
Lesson 1 ended with a follower you wrote yourself: peek at a slot, apply each committed transaction, keep a bookmark, confirm. That works for one table and one index. A payments platform has forty tables, and their changes feed a search index, a cache, the data lake's S3 bucket and three other teams' services. Kafka is the natural place to put those changes: one ordered, durable log per table that any number of consumers read at their own pace, which is what the Messaging and logs track built. What is left is the program in the middle, with batching, retries, a bookmark that survives a crash, several copies running at once, and a way to turn records into bytes and back.

Kafka Connect is that program, written once. It's a runtime that ships with Kafka, and you configure it instead of coding it. Its parts:

- A worker is a JVM process that runs Connect. In distributed mode, workers with the same `group.id` form a Connect cluster and share the work through Kafka's group protocol, the way consumers share partitions (the Messaging and logs track's lesson on consumer groups). When a worker dies, the others take over its work.
- A connector is one configured copy job: a plugin class plus settings, created with a POST to the REST API on port 8083. A source connector reads an outside system and writes to Kafka; a sink connector reads Kafka and writes out.
- A task does the copying. A connector splits its job into up to `tasks.max` tasks, and the cluster spreads them over its workers.
- A converter turns Connect's internal records into the bytes in Kafka and back: `JsonConverter`, `StringConverter`, or a registry-aware Avro converter that registers schemas for you.
- A transform (a single message transform, SMT) changes each record on the way: renames a field, masks a card number, sends the record to another topic.

Connect keeps its own state in three compacted Kafka topics: `connect-configs` for connector configurations, `connect-status` for which task runs where, and `connect-offsets` for each source connector's bookmark in its source. Kafka 4.4 (KIP-1209) adds `connect-internal-topics.sh`, so you can create those topics yourself with the settings you choose.

The source connector that matters here is **Debezium 3.7**, and its PostgreSQL connector is lesson 1's follower, built for production. It creates a slot, takes the initial snapshot, then reads the slot with `pgoutput`. Each row change becomes a change event with `before`, `after`, `op` (`c`, `u`, `d`, or `r` for a snapshot read) and `source` (the LSN, the transaction id, the table). Events go to one topic per table, `<prefix>.public.payment`, keyed by the primary key, so each row's changes stay in order in one partition. The LSN it reached is its offset in `connect-offsets`. Connect flushes that offset about once a minute (`offset.flush.interval.ms`, 60 s by default), and Debezium then confirms the LSN to the slot. Lesson 1's warnings carry over unchanged: delivery is at-least-once, and a stopped connector's slot keeps WAL.

sections.h: A change event makes your table's columns public
sections.body:
Change data capture adds a problem of its own. Debezium's events carry the table's columns, so the columns are now an API that six teams read. One morning the payment team renames `amount` to `amount_minor`, because a new currency has three decimal places, and runs the migration. Debezium follows the change, and its events now carry `amount_minor`. The ledger consumer looks for `amount`, finds nothing, and posts 0.00. Nobody gets an exception. Rolling back doesn't clean it up either: records in the new shape stay in the topic for the whole retention period, and every replay reads both shapes.

Kafka can't stop this. A broker stores a value as bytes and never looks inside it (the Messaging and logs track's lesson on the log). The Encoding track's lesson on schema evolution built the two pieces that can: a schema that says which version wrote each record, and a registry that checks every new version against the old ones before anyone writes with it. Here is how they sit in Kafka.

A registry-aware serializer (Confluent's Avro, Protobuf or JSON Schema serializer, or Connect's Avro converter for Debezium's events) registers the record's schema under a **subject**, `<topic>-value` by default, and gets back a numeric id. It writes 5 bytes before the data: a magic byte 0 and the 4-byte id. The consumer's deserializer reads the id, fetches that writer's schema once and caches it, then resolves it against its own reader's schema with Avro's rules from that lesson: a field the writer has and the reader doesn't is skipped, a field the reader has and the writer doesn't takes the reader's default, and a missing field with no default fails the read.

```java
// the consumer's side: the writer's schema comes by id, the reader's schema is the consumer's own
Schema writer = registry.schemaById(schemaIdFromTheFirst5Bytes);
var reader = new GenericDatumReader<GenericRecord>(writer, myPaymentSchema);
GenericRecord payment = reader.read(null, DecoderFactory.get().binaryDecoder(avroBytes, null));
```

```kotlin
// the consumer's side: the writer's schema comes by id, the reader's schema is the consumer's own
val writer: Schema = registry.schemaById(schemaIdFromTheFirst5Bytes)
val reader = GenericDatumReader<GenericRecord>(writer, myPaymentSchema)
val payment: GenericRecord = reader.read(null, DecoderFactory.get().binaryDecoder(avroBytes, null))
```

(`registry.schemaById` stands for what the registry-aware deserializer does for you.)

With a registry in front of the topic, the rename fails early and loudly. The converter can't register a version that old records can't be read with, so the connector's task stops with an error instead of publishing records the ledger can't read. A stopped connector is an incident, but one with an alarm, and lesson 1 told you what to watch on the database while it's down.

try.title: Read one payment with three reader schemas
steps: Run `AvroEvolutionDemo` from the `labs` folder (command below). No broker, no registry: Avro's own library on your JVM.
It writes a payment with schema v1, then reads the same bytes with v1, with v2 (adds `currency` with a default) and with v3 (adds `merchantId` with none). Predict which reads fail before it prints.

code.title: AvroEvolutionDemo.java

alt.title: AvroEvolutionDemo.kt
alt.src:
package sfz.stream.l02.demo

import org.apache.avro.Schema
import org.apache.avro.SchemaCompatibility
import org.apache.avro.generic.GenericData
import org.apache.avro.generic.GenericDatumReader
import org.apache.avro.generic.GenericDatumWriter
import org.apache.avro.generic.GenericRecord
import org.apache.avro.io.DecoderFactory
import org.apache.avro.io.EncoderFactory
import java.io.ByteArrayOutputStream
import java.nio.ByteBuffer
import java.util.HexFormat

private const val V1 = """
{"type": "record", "name": "Payment", "fields": [
  {"name": "id", "type": "string"},
  {"name": "account", "type": "string"},
  {"name": "amount", "type": "long"}]}"""
private const val V2 = """
{"type": "record", "name": "Payment", "fields": [
  {"name": "id", "type": "string"},
  {"name": "account", "type": "string"},
  {"name": "amount", "type": "long"},
  {"name": "currency", "type": "string", "default": "EUR"}]}"""
private const val V3 = """
{"type": "record", "name": "Payment", "fields": [
  {"name": "id", "type": "string"},
  {"name": "account", "type": "string"},
  {"name": "amount", "type": "long"},
  {"name": "merchantId", "type": "string"}]}"""

/**
 * One payment, written with version 1 of its Avro schema and read back with three reader schemas: the same one,
 * one that adds a field with a default, and one that adds a field without a default. No broker, no registry.
 */
fun main() {
    val v1 = Schema.Parser().parse(V1)
    val v2 = Schema.Parser().parse(V2)
    val v3 = Schema.Parser().parse(V3)

    // the producer's side: a v1 payment, encoded as Avro binary
    val payment = GenericData.Record(v1).apply { put("id", "pay-1"); put("account", "acct-17"); put("amount", 4000L) }
    val out = ByteArrayOutputStream()
    val encoder = EncoderFactory.get().binaryEncoder(out, null)
    GenericDatumWriter<GenericRecord>(v1).write(payment, encoder)
    encoder.flush()
    val avro = out.toByteArray()
    println("v1 payment as Avro binary, ${avro.size} bytes: ${HexFormat.ofDelimiter(" ").formatHex(avro)}")

    // what a registry-aware serializer sends: magic byte 0, the schema id (say 1) as 4 bytes, then the Avro bytes
    val framed = ByteBuffer.allocate(5 + avro.size).put(0).putInt(1).put(avro).array()
    println("with the 5-byte registry prefix, ${framed.size} bytes: ${HexFormat.ofDelimiter(" ").formatHex(framed, 0, 5)} | ...")

    // the consumer's side: the writer schema comes with the data (by id), the reader schema is the consumer's own
    for ((name, reader) in listOf("v1" to v1, "v2" to v2, "v3" to v3)) {
        try {
            val read = GenericDatumReader<GenericRecord>(v1, reader).read(null, DecoderFactory.get().binaryDecoder(avro, null))
            println("reader $name reads it: $read")
        } catch (e: Exception) {
            println("reader $name fails:    ${e.javaClass.simpleName}: ${e.message}")
        }
    }
    // Avro's own check, the one a registry runs before it accepts a new version
    println("can v2 read v1 data? ${SchemaCompatibility.checkReaderWriterCompatibility(v2, v1).type}")
    println("can v3 read v1 data? ${SchemaCompatibility.checkReaderWriterCompatibility(v3, v1).type}")
}

try.expect:
```text
v1 payment as Avro binary, 16 bytes: 0a 70 61 79 2d 31 0e 61 63 63 74 2d 31 37 c0 3e
with the 5-byte registry prefix, 21 bytes: 00 00 00 00 01 | ...
reader v1 reads it: {"id": "pay-1", "account": "acct-17", "amount": 4000}
reader v2 reads it: {"id": "pay-1", "account": "acct-17", "amount": 4000, "currency": "EUR"}
reader v3 fails:    AvroTypeException: Found Payment, expecting Payment, missing required field merchantId
can v2 read v1 data? COMPATIBLE
can v3 read v1 data? INCOMPATIBLE
```
The 16 bytes hold no field names: `0a` is the length of "pay-1" (5, which Avro's zigzag encoding stores as 10, hex `0a`), then its five bytes; `0e` and "acct-17"; `c0 3e` is 4000 as a variable-length long. The registry prefix adds a 0 byte and the schema id. Reader v2 filled `currency` from its default; reader v3 had nothing to fill `merchantId` with. Avro's `SchemaCompatibility` gives the same verdicts as the reads.

sections.h: The registry refuses a breaking version, in the direction you choose
sections.body:
Before it registers a version, the registry runs the Encoding track's check in the direction the subject's **compatibility mode** names. One line each, as a reminder: BACKWARD, the default, means the new schema can read data written with the latest one, so consumers upgrade first. FORWARD means readers on the latest version can read data written with the new one, so producers upgrade first. FULL means both. Each has a `_TRANSITIVE` twin that checks every registered version, which a compacted topic needs, because its version 1 records never age out.

The Kafka-specific part is choosing the mode per topic, and the question that decides it is: who changes first?

- Events your service designs, such as `payments-value`. Your team can roll consumers before producers, so BACKWARD fits, or BACKWARD_TRANSITIVE if the topic is compacted.
- CDC topics. The database changes first: a migration is the producer change, and every consumer meets the new shape at once. That calls for FORWARD or FULL, because old consumers must read new records. Dropping a nullable column then passes, since old readers fill it with null. Dropping or renaming a NOT NULL column is refused. Renaming a nullable column passes, and old consumers quietly read null: the registry checks shapes, not meaning, as the Encoding track warned.

Then make the registry the only way in:

- Set `auto.register.schemas=false` on production producers and register schemas from CI after review. Otherwise any deploy registers whatever its code happens to say.
- In CI, POST the candidate to `/compatibility/subjects/<subject>/versions/latest` and fail the build on `false`.
- A refused registration comes back as HTTP 409 with error code 40901 and a reason such as READER_FIELD_MISSING_DEFAULT_VALUE.

The stepper shows one check under the default mode, and the Try it runs the same checks against a real registry.

try.title: Ask a real registry
steps: From the `labs` folder, start the broker with Schema Registry: `docker compose -f env/kafka.yml --profile schemas up -d --wait`. The registry takes about a minute the first time.
Run `RegistryDemo` (command below). It reads the global mode, registers v1, checks and registers v2, then checks and tries to register v3, all over the REST API.
Predict the HTTP status of the last POST before you run it.

alt.src:
package sfz.stream.l02.demo

import java.net.URI
import java.net.http.HttpClient
import java.net.http.HttpRequest
import java.net.http.HttpResponse

private const val REGISTRY = "http://localhost:8081"
private val http: HttpClient = HttpClient.newHttpClient()

private const val V1_SCHEMA = """
{"type": "record", "name": "Payment", "fields": [
  {"name": "id", "type": "string"}, {"name": "account", "type": "string"}, {"name": "amount", "type": "long"}]}"""
private const val V2_SCHEMA = """
{"type": "record", "name": "Payment", "fields": [
  {"name": "id", "type": "string"}, {"name": "account", "type": "string"}, {"name": "amount", "type": "long"},
  {"name": "currency", "type": "string", "default": "EUR"}]}"""
private const val V3_SCHEMA = """
{"type": "record", "name": "Payment", "fields": [
  {"name": "id", "type": "string"}, {"name": "account", "type": "string"}, {"name": "amount", "type": "long"},
  {"name": "currency", "type": "string", "default": "EUR"}, {"name": "merchantId", "type": "string"}]}"""

/**
 * Talks to Schema Registry on localhost:8081 over its REST API: registers version 1 of a payment schema, then asks
 * whether two changes are compatible under the subject's mode, and tries to register both.
 */
fun main() {
    // one subject per run; the serializer's default name for a topic's values is "<topic>-value"
    val subject = "payments-${System.currentTimeMillis() % 100_000}-value"
    call("GET", "/config")
    call("POST", "/subjects/$subject/versions", V1_SCHEMA)                                    // register v1
    call("POST", "/compatibility/subjects/$subject/versions/latest", V2_SCHEMA)               // v2: adds currency, with a default
    call("POST", "/subjects/$subject/versions", V2_SCHEMA)
    call("POST", "/compatibility/subjects/$subject/versions/latest?verbose=true", V3_SCHEMA)  // v3: adds merchantId, no default
    call("POST", "/subjects/$subject/versions", V3_SCHEMA)
    call("GET", "/subjects/$subject/versions")
}

private fun call(method: String, path: String, avroSchema: String? = null) {
    val request = HttpRequest.newBuilder(URI.create(REGISTRY + path)).header("Content-Type", "application/vnd.schemaregistry.v1+json")
    if (avroSchema == null) request.GET() else request.POST(HttpRequest.BodyPublishers.ofString("{\"schema\": ${quote(avroSchema)}}"))
    val response = http.send(request.build(), HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString())
    val line = "$method $path\n  -> ${response.statusCode()} ${summary(response.body())}"
    println(line.replace(Regex("payments-\\d+-value"), "payments-value")) // the subject has this run's number
}

/** The parts of a reply worth reading: ids, verdicts and the reason a change was refused. */
private fun summary(body: String): String {
    val reason = Regex("errorType:\\\\?\"(\\w+)\\\\?\", description:\\\\?\"([^\"\\\\]+)").find(body)
    val head = body.replace(Regex("\"schema\":\".*\""), "\"schema\":...").replace(Regex(",\"messages\":.*|, details: .*|,\"guid\":\"[^\"]*\""), "")
    return if (reason != null) "$head  [${reason.groupValues[1]}: ${reason.groupValues[2]}]" else head
}

private fun quote(json: String) = "\"" + json.trim().replace("\\", "\\\\").replace("\"", "\\\"").replace("\n", " ") + "\""

sections.h: The outbox: publish events you designed, in the same transaction
sections.body:
The payment service authorizes a payment, inserts a row into PostgreSQL, and must tell the ledger: `PaymentAuthorized`. Lesson 1's tools give two options, and both fall short. A `producer.send` after the insert is a dual write: a crash between the two loses the event, and sending first announces a payment that may never commit. The Messaging and logs track's lesson on transactions showed that a Kafka transaction can't include the database, and KIP-939's two-phase commit hasn't shipped. Plain CDC on the `payment` table avoids the dual write, but it publishes row changes in the table's own shape, the problem of section 2. And an UPDATE of `status` says nothing about intent: was the payment captured, or corrected by an operator?

The **transactional outbox** fixes both. The service inserts the payment row and an event row into an `outbox` table in the same database transaction, so both commit or neither does. The outbox row has its own schema, designed for consumers, and it changes only when you decide. It is still two writes, but both go to one database in one transaction, which is the one place where atomic commit is cheap. Debezium then captures only the outbox table.

A simple poller could move the rows instead: `SELECT * FROM outbox WHERE sent = false` every second, publish, mark as sent. That's a query per second on the payments database, up to a second of delay, and an ordering trap. Rows become visible in commit order, not id order, so a poller that pages by id skips a row whose transaction committed late. Reading the WAL has no such gap, because decoding hands out transactions in commit order (lesson 1).

Debezium's outbox event router turns each outbox insert into a record on `outbox.event.<aggregatetype>`, keyed by `aggregateid`, with the payload as the value and the event id in a header named `id`. With the account as `aggregateid`, each account's events keep their order in one partition. The costs are extra writes on the payments database and rows to clean up; the router ignores deletes, so the service can delete each outbox row right after inserting it, in the same transaction, and the table stays empty.

Delivery is still at-least-once. Connect flushes the LSN about once a minute, and after a crash in between, Debezium sends the events since the last flush again, with the same ids. So consumers dedupe on the event id, in the same transaction as their own effect (the Messaging and logs track's lesson on consumers).

analogy: A schema is the printed form a payment slip uses: named boxes in a fixed order. The registry is the office that approves new versions of the form, and its rule (BACKWARD) is that a clerk holding the new form must still be able to read every old slip in the archive; a new box is fine if the form says what to assume when it's empty. The outbox is a carbon set: the branch writes the payment and the courier's note on the same sheet, so one can't exist without the other. CDC is the courier reading the carbon copies in the order they were stamped and remembering the last stamp number. The analogy breaks at the courier: after losing its place, Debezium may deliver a note twice, so head office must recognise a note by its number.
in_your_world: Your services write to Oracle, and the same pattern works there: Debezium's Oracle connector reads the redo log through LogMiner, and the outbox event router doesn't care which database fed it. A Quarkus service can write the outbox row in the same JTA transaction as the payment (Debezium also ships a Quarkus outbox extension that does this from a CDI event). A Temporal activity that writes a payment and must announce it should write the outbox row in its own database transaction, not call a Kafka producer. On the schema side, register schemas from CI and set `auto.register.schemas=false` on producers, so a deploy can't slip a new version past review; use FORWARD or FULL on CDC topics, where the database changes first, and BACKWARD_TRANSITIVE on compacted topics such as account state, where version 1 records never go away.
mistake: Unblocking a deploy by setting the subject's compatibility to NONE. The registry refused the new schema for a reason: some consumer, or some old record in the topic, can't be read with it. With NONE the version goes in, the producer deploys, and the failure moves to a consumer at 3 a.m., or to the replay next month. The fix is to make the change compatible: give the new field a default, or rename in two steps (add the new field with a default, move readers over, remove the old field later). Run the compatibility check in CI against the real registry, and keep `auto.register.schemas=false` in production producers so that only reviewed versions get registered.

lab.title: Build the registry's compatibility check and the outbox relay
steps: Run the tests from the `labs` folder. All 15 fail. They need no Docker: the schema tests compare your rule with Avro's own `SchemaCompatibility`, and the outbox tests replay what Debezium did in the Try-it.

In `CompatibilityChecker.kt`, write `readProblems(reader, writer)`: names must match; then for every reader field, a type the writer's type can't be promoted to is a `TYPE_MISMATCH`, and a field the writer lacks with no default is a `READER_FIELD_MISSING_DEFAULT_VALUE`. `canPromote` is given.
Write `check(mode, candidate, registered)`: pick the latest version or all of them, and run `readProblems` in the direction each mode asks for.

In `OutboxRelay.java`, write `route` (outbox inserts and snapshot reads only; topic, key, value and the `id` and `eventType` headers) and `relay` (collect changes per transaction, route them at commit, drop rollbacks, skip commits at or below the stored LSN). Run until all 15 pass.
hints: BACKWARD is `readProblems(reader = candidate, writer = latest)`; FORWARD swaps the two. FULL is both, backward first.
In `relay`, a `LinkedHashMap<Long, List<ChangeEvent>>` from transaction id to its changes is enough; the commit entry says when to emit them.
`record.headers().add("id", bytes)` adds a header to a `ProducerRecord`; add `id` before `eventType`.

recap: Kafka Connect runs copy jobs so you don't write them: workers form a cluster, connectors split into tasks, converters turn records into bytes, transforms edit them, and source offsets live in `connect-offsets`.

Debezium's PostgreSQL connector is lesson 1's follower for a whole database: slot, snapshot, change events (`before`, `after`, `op`, `source`) on a topic per table keyed by primary key, and the LSN as its offset.
CDC makes a table's columns public. A registry-aware serializer puts a 0 byte and a 4-byte schema id before each record, and the registry checks every new version before it is used.

Pick the compatibility mode by who changes first: BACKWARD for events your consumers can roll ahead of producers, FORWARD or FULL for CDC topics, `_TRANSITIVE` for compacted topics. Keep `auto.register.schemas=false` in production.
The transactional outbox writes the business row and an event row in one database transaction; Debezium's outbox router publishes it keyed by `aggregateid`, in commit order.
It stays at-least-once: after a crash Debezium repeats events since the last offset flush with the same ids, so consumers dedupe on the event id.

quiz.q: From lesson 1: when a Debezium PostgreSQL connector starts for the first time, why must it create its replication slot before it reads the tables for the initial snapshot?
options: PostgreSQL won't let a session read a table while no slot exists
So that the snapshot can skip rows the slot already holds
So that every change committed while the snapshot runs is kept in the slot; read the tables first and a write in between is in neither
The order doesn't matter, because each change carries the whole row
quiz.why: A slot keeps only changes committed after it was created. Create it first, and a write during the copy is in the slot for sure, maybe also in the copy, which is harmless because each change carries the whole row. Read the tables first, and a write that commits before the slot exists is lost to every consumer. Full rows make the overlap harmless; they don't rescue a write that is in neither.

quiz.q: A Debezium topic for the `payment` table uses Schema Registry. The DBA drops the nullable column `note` and then the NOT NULL column `channel`. Which compatibility mode lets old consumers keep reading, and what happens to each change under it?
options: FORWARD: dropping `note` passes because old readers fill it with null; dropping `channel` is refused because old readers have no default for it
BACKWARD: both drops pass, and old consumers keep working
FORWARD: both drops are refused
NONE: it's the only mode that allows dropping columns
quiz.why: On a CDC topic the producer changes first, so the question is whether old readers can read new records: FORWARD. Old readers have `note` as an optional field with a null default, so they read null; they have `channel` as a required field with no default, so the registry refuses that version and the connector stops loudly. BACKWARD accepts both drops, because it only asks whether new readers can read old data, and the old consumers then fail on `channel`.

quiz.q: A team switches a subject to FORWARD. In which order should producers and consumers move to the next version?
options: Consumers first, then producers
Producers first, then consumers
Both at once, in one deploy
It doesn't matter in FORWARD
quiz.why: FORWARD guarantees that readers on the latest registered schema can read data written with the new one. So producers can start writing the new version while consumers still run the old one. Under BACKWARD it's the other way round, and only FULL makes the order free.

quiz.q: In PostgreSQL, transaction A inserts an outbox row first, then transaction B inserts one, then B commits, then A commits. In which order does Debezium write their events?
options: A, then B: in the order the rows were inserted
In outbox id order
In any order: CDC doesn't keep order
B, then A: in commit order
quiz.why: Logical decoding hands over a transaction when it commits, with its changes in order, so transactions come out in commit order. That's also why a poller that reads by id can skip A: B's higher id was visible first.

quiz.q: A Debezium connector writes events for 40 seconds after its last offset flush, then its worker crashes. What do consumers of `outbox.event.payment` see after the restart?
options: Nothing changes: Debezium confirms each event to PostgreSQL first
Some events a second time, with the same event ids
A gap: those 40 seconds of events are lost
The same events with new ids
quiz.why: The restarted task reads the WAL again from the last stored LSN, so the events after it are written again. The slot kept that WAL, so nothing is lost, and the ids come from the outbox rows, so they repeat. Consumers dedupe on the `id` header.

explain_back.prompt: A colleague's payment service inserts the payment into PostgreSQL and then calls `producer.send`. Explain what can go wrong, why a retry or a Kafka transaction doesn't fix it, and how the outbox with Debezium does.
explain_back.answer: They are two writes to two systems with nothing tying them together. A crash after the insert and before the send leaves a payment that no consumer hears about; sending first leaves an event for a payment that may never commit. After a crash the service doesn't know which half happened, so a retry can't put it right. A Kafka transaction only covers Kafka writes and offsets, and the two-phase commit proposal, KIP-939, isn't released. With the outbox, the service writes the payment row and an event row in one PostgreSQL transaction, so both exist or neither does. Debezium, running in Kafka Connect, reads the committed rows from the write-ahead log through a replication slot, in commit order (lesson 1's follower), and the outbox event router publishes each event with the account as key. Rolled-back transactions never reach the log reader. Debezium can repeat events after a crash, because it stores its WAL position only about once a minute, so the consumers dedupe on the event id in the same transaction as their own effect.

deeper.body:
**The schemas Debezium registers.** The Avro converter builds each table's schema from its columns. A NOT NULL column becomes a required field; a nullable one becomes `["null", type]` with a null default. That is why, under FORWARD, dropping a nullable column passes and dropping a NOT NULL one doesn't.

**Optional fields in your own events.** A field that may be missing is a union with null and a null default: `{"name": "note", "type": ["null", "string"], "default": null}`. The default must match the first type in the union, which is why `null` comes first.

**Subject names.** The default `TopicNameStrategy` gives one schema per topic (`payments-value`). `RecordNameStrategy` and `TopicRecordNameStrategy` name the subject after the record type, so one topic can carry several event types, each with its own evolution, for example `PaymentAuthorized` and `PaymentCaptured` on one partition to keep their order.

**The initial snapshot.** When a Debezium connector starts with no stored offset, `snapshot.mode=initial` reads the captured tables first and emits each existing row as a read event (`op` = `r`), slot first and copy second, as lesson 1 explained. That's why the Try-it's topic started with the row from the WAL peek. For an outbox you usually want only new rows: set `snapshot.mode=no_data`.

**Oracle.** Debezium's Oracle connector reads redo logs through LogMiner by default. The model is the same, a log of committed changes read with a stored position (an SCN instead of an LSN), with more setup: supplemental logging and a LogMiner user.
